cards.name: Meeting minutes
cards.summary: The official record of a meeting: who attended, what was decided (in the exact words of each resolution), who disagreed, and who will do what by when. Good minutes are a fair and correct summary of decisions and reasons, not a transcript of who said what.
use_for: board and committee minutes for private and public companies (with the company secretary)
managing-committee minutes for housing societies, RWAs, trusts, NGOs and school boards
client-call MoM (minutes of meeting) an agency sends after a kickoff or review
internal project or leadership meeting action logs
avoid: Writing a transcript ('Mr Sharma said... then Ms Rao said...'): readers cannot find the decision. Record the decision, the reason in one line, and dissent by name; drop the back-and-forth.
Editorialising ('a heated debate', 'the treasurer angrily objected'): minutes can be read out in a dispute or a court. Use neutral verbs: 'raised', 'objected', 'recorded dissent'.
Action items without an owner or a date ('Website to be updated'): nobody does them. Every action gets one named owner and a due date.
Using the minutes to add things that were not discussed or decided. If it was not decided in the room, it goes in a follow-up email, not the minutes.

sources.title: TaxGuru: Secretarial Standards on minutes (SS-1 & SS-2)
sources.supports: secondary summary of ICSI SS-1: minutes are a fair and correct summary, not a transcript; draft circulated within 15 days, comments within 7 days, final entry within 30 days

buyers: company secretaries and CS firms (board and general meeting minutes)
housing societies, RWAs, trusts, NGOs and school managing committees
agencies and consultancies that send MoM after client meetings
founders' offices and chiefs of staff
cards.value_why: Routine company-secretarial and admin work, usually done in-house; Indian board minutes follow ICSI SS-1 (TaxGuru summary), which is why a CS signs them off rather than a freelance writer.
cards.goal: Anyone who missed the meeting can see exactly what was decided and which action they own, by when, and the record holds up if the decision is questioned later.

structure.does: Organisation name, type and serial number of the meeting (e.g. '7th Managing Committee Meeting'), date, start and end time, venue or video link.
Present (names and roles), in attendance (invitees, staff), leave of absence granted, quorum present yes/no, who chaired.
Confirmation of the last meeting's minutes and status of its open actions (done / carried forward with new date).

Item number and title; 1-2 lines of background; the gist of discussion only where it explains the decision; the decision or resolution in exact final wording ('RESOLVED THAT...' for boards, 'Decided:' for committees); dissent or abstention recorded by name if asked.
Table: action, owner (one name), due date, linked agenda item. Pulls every action from the items above.
Date, time and venue of the next meeting; time the meeting closed; space for the chair's signature and date where minutes are signed.

length.note: Driven by the number of agenda items, not the meeting's duration. A 30-minute client call is 150-300 words of MoM; a board meeting with 8 resolutions runs long because resolutions are recorded in full.

checklist: Does the header give meeting type, serial number, date, time and venue or link?
Are attendees, leave of absence and quorum stated?
Does every agenda item end in a clearly marked decision, resolution or 'deferred to [date]'?
Are resolutions written in their final exact wording rather than paraphrased?
Is any dissent or abstention recorded by name where a member asked for it?
Does every action have exactly one named owner and a due date?
Is the action log consistent with the items (no action in the log that is not in an item, and vice versa)?
Is the language free of opinion words about people ('heated', 'angrily', 'rudely')?
Are amounts, dates and names written in full and consistent throughout (Rs 4,50,000, not 'approx 4.5L' in one place and '450k' in another)?
Is the next meeting's date given or marked 'to be fixed'?
pitfalls: Circulating late: memories fade and disputes grow. For Indian board minutes, SS-1 (per the TaxGuru summary) expects the draft out within 15 days; for client MoM, send the same day.
Mixing who-said-what with decisions so the decision is buried in paragraph three. Put the decision on its own labelled line under each item.
Vague owners ('team', 'admin', 'all members'). Name one person; others can be listed as support.

Recording sensitive personal remarks (health, family, salary of a named employee) in minutes that go to a wide list. Record the decision and keep personal detail in a confidential annexure if it must be kept.

require.label: has an owner or due date for actions

cards.exemplar_brief: Minutes of the 7th monthly managing-committee meeting of a 240-flat housing society in Noida Sector 75: 6 members present, quorum met; items: confirmation of last minutes, lift AMC renewal (approved at Rs 1,85,000 with one member's dissent recorded), monsoon waterlogging complaint (secretary to get two contractor quotes by 15 November), festival budget (deferred). English; 400-650 words; ends with an action log table (action, owner, due date) and next meeting date.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Every part in order: header (type, serial no., date, time, venue), attendance with leave of absence, invitee and quorum, previous minutes confirmed, each item with background / discussion only where it explains / a labelled 'Decided:' or 'Deferred' line, dissent recorded by name with its ground, 3-row action log (one owner, due date, item link), next meeting and signature line. Neutral language, Rs 1,85,000 consistent, weekdays correct. Writer faults: Facility Manager is listed 'in attendance for item 3 only' but speaks under item 4 (waterlogging); action 1 (sign the AMC by 31 October) is in the log but not in item 3's decision text, which breaks the card's log-matches-items rule.

cards.name: Meme and meme-caption content
cards.summary: A meme template (image, panel or short video format the audience already knows) plus on-image text and a caption that makes a brand or page part of a joke people want to send to a friend. Good brand memes are funny without the brand, and the brand sits inside the joke instead of a logo stuck on top.
use_for: brand memes for a D2C, fintech, edtech or OTT handle's own feed
paid placements on meme-page networks (Hindi, Hinglish and regional pages)
moment-marketing memes on a trending format or news moment (see genre:newsjacking_post)
satire and commentary pages that post memes daily
avoid: Explaining the joke in the caption ('Because who doesn't love saving money? 😂'): it kills the laugh. The caption adds a second beat, a tag prompt or nothing.
Logo-slapping: a meme with the product shot or offer pasted in reads as an ad and gets scrolled past. Make the product a natural object or situation inside the joke.
Memes on deaths, disasters, accidents, communal incidents or someone's caste, religion, region, body or disability. Skip the moment, or post a plain, respectful note instead.

Reposting another page's meme with a new watermark: Instagram treats accounts whose posts in a 30-day window are mostly reposts as aggregators and stops recommending them. Make an original take on the format.
A dead template: a format the audience has seen for months reads as a brand trying too hard. Check the format is still circulating on the target page's feed this week.

social media and meme-marketing agencies running page networks
film and web-series promotion teams
satire, campus and city meme pages
cards.value_why: At least two Indian agencies (Elevate Network, Idiotic Media) sell meme marketing as a service through networks of meme pages, increasingly in Hindi and regional languages; both are vendor sources, so demand is real but its size is unmeasured.
cards.goal: Send or tag the meme to a friend (shares, tags, saves) while remembering which brand or page made it.

structure.does: Name the template or format and why it fits (the emotion it carries: betrayal, smugness, expectation vs reality, POV). Describe the image or panels in [brackets] for the designer.
Top text or first panel: the relatable situation in the audience's own words and language (Hinglish for most Indian youth pages).
Bottom text, second panel or label: the twist. The brand, product or category appears here only if it IS the twist.
Either a second beat that extends the joke, a tag prompt aimed at a specific friend type ('Tag the friend who...'), or empty. Never an explanation or a sales line.
Platform paid-partnership label plus an upfront label in the caption when a brand paid the page.
One plain line describing the image and its text for screen readers.

length.note: On-image text plus caption. Shorter is funnier; multi-panel formats and carousel memes earn the top of the range. Text on the image must stay readable on a phone without zooming.

checklist: Is the joke funny to someone who has never heard of the brand?
Is the template or format named and described so a designer can build it?
Is the punchline in the last panel or last words, not the first?
Does the brand or product appear at most once, as part of the joke rather than a logo or offer pasted on?
Is the caption free of any explanation of the joke and of hard-sell lines (buy now, use code, limited offer)?
Is the on-image text short enough to read on a phone (no panel with a paragraph)?
Does it avoid tragedy, death, communal events and jokes at someone's caste, religion, region, gender, body or disability?
If a brand paid for it, is there an upfront paid-partnership disclosure?
Is it an original take rather than a repost of another page's meme?
Is the language the target page's own (Hinglish, Hindi, regional) rather than translated brand English?
pitfalls: Approval chains: a meme that needs three rounds of brand approval misses its moment. Agree upfront what the page can post without sign-off (tone, banned topics) and what needs review.

Using film stills, celebrity photos or another creator's image as the template on a paid post: personality-rights and copyright claims land on the brand. Prefer widely used generic templates, own photography or illustration, or licensed stills.
Writing the caption in brand English on a Hinglish page: it marks the post as an ad instantly. Write the way the page's admin writes.
Political or religious memes on a brand account: one screenshot becomes a boycott thread. Keep brand memes to everyday life, work, exams, food, traffic and family.

ban.label: explains its own joke
ban.regex: (?i)get it\?|see what we did there|because who doesn'?t love

cards.exemplar_brief: Paid meme for a fictional Bengaluru UPI bill-splitting app ('SplitKaro') placed on a Hinglish college meme page (audience 18-24, metros and tier-2 cities). Deliver: template described in [brackets], on-image setup and punch text, caption under 25 words with a tag-a-friend prompt, 'Paid partnership' disclosure, alt text. Topic: the friend who says 'baad mein UPI kar dunga' and never does. No hard-sell line, no discount code.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Original two-panel illustration named with its emotion and bracketed panel brief; setup is the friend's own line, punch ''Baad mein' = convocation ke baad' lands last; caption is a second beat (SplitKaro request seen 2:14 am, 'typing... 18 mahine se') plus 'Tag karo apna Dev'; brand appears once inside the joke, no hard sell; 'Paid partnership' upfront; alt text present. Funny without the brand, natural Hinglish. Nit: panel 2 brief gives no expression or text placement for the designer; the punch is solid rather than a killer line.

cards.name: Brand messaging framework / message house
cards.summary: The internal source document every piece of copy is written from: who the brand serves, the one umbrella message, three or four message pillars, and the proof behind each, plus approved boilerplates and words to use or avoid. Good frameworks are specific enough that a new writer can produce on-message copy without asking the founder, and every claim has a proof point next to it.
use_for: pre-work before a website rewrite, rebrand or launch campaign
onboarding a new agency, freelancer or sales hire to a brand
aligning founders, sales and marketing on one story after a pivot
a deliverable inside a brand strategy or positioning engagement
avoid: Pillars that are adjectives ('Innovative', 'Reliable', 'Customer-first'): every competitor claims them. Write each pillar as a claim a competitor could not copy-paste, e.g. 'GST notices tracked from the day they are issued, not the day you find them'.
Proof points left as 'TBD' forever: copy written from the framework then makes unsupported claims. Mark missing proof '[proof needed: X]' and list who will supply it.
Writing it as finished ad copy. It is an internal reference: plain sentences, one idea each, no taglines doing the work of explanations.
One message for every audience. Add a segment matrix so the CFO and the end user each get the pillar that matters to them.

cards.value_why: Sold as a fixed-price 'brand messaging guide' on B2B rate cards (Mighty Fine Copy) and listed by AWAI as 'Key Message Copy Platform'; Upwork's In-Demand Skills 2026 names Brand Strategy among the fastest-growing marketing skills (+26%).
cards.goal: Every writer, salesperson and agency who touches the brand writes copy from the same audience, umbrella message, pillars and proof, without asking the founder.

structure.does: Who the brand serves (segments), the problem in the customer's own words (quote interviews or reviews), and what they use today instead.
For [target] who [need], [brand] is the [category] that [key benefit], unlike [alternative], because [proof/reason].
The single idea every piece of copy must leave behind, in plain words a customer would repeat.
3-4 pillars, each: a claim headline, 2-3 sentences of explanation, and 2-4 proof points (numbers, named customers, certifications, product facts) with their source.
Per persona or buyer role: their top pain, the pillar to lead with, one key message, the typical objection and the next step to ask for.
The brand described at three lengths for reuse: about 10 words, about 50 words, about 100 words.
The 4-6 objections sales hears most, each with the approved answer and its proof.
3-4 voice traits with do/don't examples; words to use (customer vocabulary) and words to avoid (jargon, competitor terms, claims legal has not cleared).

length.note: One audience and one product sits near the low end; multiple segments, products or markets push it up. If it passes 4,000 words, split per product line.

checklist: Is there exactly one umbrella message, in one sentence under 25 words?
Are there 3-4 pillars, each a specific claim rather than an adjective?
Does every pillar have at least two proof points, or a marked '[proof needed]' slot naming what is missing?
Does the audience section use customer language (quotes, review phrases), not internal jargon?
Does the positioning statement name the alternative the customer uses today?
Is there a segment matrix mapping each buyer role to a lead pillar and a next step?
Are boilerplates given at three lengths and consistent with each other?
Do the objection answers each cite a proof point?
Are 'best', 'No. 1', 'only' and percentage claims either substantiated or removed?
Could a new freelancer write a homepage hero from this document alone?
pitfalls: Writing it from the founder's pitch only: the framework then repeats what the team wants to say, not what buyers care about. Mine 10-20 customer reviews, sales-call notes or support tickets first.
Too many pillars (6-8): nobody remembers them and copy tries to say everything. Merge until there are 3-4.

Claims that legal or compliance would block (guaranteed savings, 'India's No. 1'): ASCI's Code requires claims of objectively ascertainable fact to be substantiated. Keep only claims with evidence on file.
Delivering it and walking away: the framework fails when nobody uses it. End with 2-3 worked examples (a homepage hero, a cold-email opener, a LinkedIn post) written from it.

ban.label: empty corporate claims outside a 'Words to avoid' list (search for: world-class, best-in-class, cutting-edge, one-stop solution, synergy, next-gen)

cards.exemplar_brief: Brand messaging framework for 'NoticeDesk' (fictional), a Jaipur SaaS that tracks GST and income-tax notices for CA firms with 3-30 staff; audience: CA partners and article managers in tier-2 cities who today track notices in Excel and WhatsApp; English; 1,200-1,800 words; positioning statement, one umbrella message, 3 pillars with proof slots marked [proof needed] where data is not supplied, segment matrix (partner vs staff), 3 boilerplate lengths, 4 objections, words to use/avoid.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C2. Complete and usable by a new freelancer: two-role audience with today's alternative (Excel + WhatsApp), positioning naming the alternative, one 15-word umbrella, 3 claim-headline pillars each with a product fact plus marked [proof needed] slots, partner/staff matrix with lead pillar, objection and next step, consistent 10/50/100-word boilerplates, 4 objections each with a proof slot, voice traits with do/don't, word lists, and a worked homepage hero. Customer-language block is a proof slot, correctly not invented. Only soft spot: objection 3's 'approved answer' is an instruction, because no security facts were given. The lint fail is the card's: the ban regex fired on 'world-class' inside the required words-to-avoid list. CARD FIX: lint.ban 'empty corporate claims' -> exempt lines under a 'Words to avoid' / 'Don't' heading (or drop world-class/one-stop solution from this card's ban list), because the card's own structure requires naming those words. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_b): lint.ban 'empty corporate claims' now ignores banned words that appear after a 'Words to avoid' / 'Don't' heading line (the card's own structure requires naming them there); re-judge pending.

cards.name: Vertical micro-drama episode script
cards.summary: The script for one 1-3 minute episode of a vertical (9:16) serial drama: it opens mid-conflict, turns the situation once, and ends on a cliffhanger that makes the viewer unlock or swipe to the next episode. Good episodes are built from close-ups, short dialogue and one clear power shift; they are written as part of a season grid, never one-off.
use_for: episodes for Indian micro-drama apps (Kuku TV, QuickTV and others) and production houses supplying them
YouTube Shorts series and Instagram reel serials
brand-funded micro-series where a D2C or fintech product lives inside the story
AI-generated micro-drama slates where the script also drives image and video prompts
avoid: Opening with setup (a character waking up, a wide shot of the city): viewers swipe in the first seconds. Open on the slap, the reveal, the humiliation or the secret, and explain later.
Recapping the last episode with narration. Re-establish the stakes inside the first scene's action or one line of dialogue.
Ending on a resolved moment. The last 3-5 seconds must open a question (a door opens, a name is read out, a phone screen is shown) and cut before the answer.
Wide shots and crowd scenes: on a phone they read as noise and they cost money. Write for close-ups and two-shots; one or two characters per frame.
Writing a feature-film scene and cutting it into 90-second pieces. Each episode needs its own hook, turn and cliffhanger; use genre:web_series_episode for longer episodic TV.

cards.value_why: Indian micro-drama apps are commissioning episodic vertical series, including AI-assisted slates (Storyboard18; Tech Times 2026-08-04 on ShareChat's $10.5M bet); Redseer via Storyboard18 forecasts the Indian market growing about 10x by FY32, and YouTube reports microdramas past 6.5 billion views (2026-09-23).
cards.goal: Watch to the last second and go straight to the next episode (swipe, unlock or follow the series).

structure.does: Series title, episode number, target duration, location and characters in the episode, and the one question this episode leaves open.
Conflict already in motion: an action or a line that shocks, humiliates, reveals or threatens. For episode 2 onward it picks up from the last cliffhanger's answer, or a twist on it.
Who wants what and what they lose if they fail, shown through one exchange, a phone screen, or a look; no narrated backstory.
One obstacle and one power shift (the underdog wins a round, or the villain gains leverage). 2-4 very short scenes, each with a scene heading.
The single twist or reversal of the episode: a reveal, a betrayal, a misunderstanding cleared or created.
Cut on an open question: a reaction close-up, an unread message, a name about to be spoken. If the app locks episodes after a free run, the biggest reveal goes on the last free episode.
On-screen text cues, key props, shot sizes (CU, MCU, two-shot), and if AI-generated, a one-line visual note per scene for the prompt writer.

length.note: Per episode script including scene headings and action lines. Duration is set by the platform (roughly 1-3 minutes per episode in trade coverage; confirm per app). Time a read-aloud of the dialogue to calibrate.

checklist: Does something shocking, tense or revealing happen in the first line or action?
Is every scene marked with a heading (INT./EXT., place, time) and kept to one or two characters in frame?
Are dialogue lines short enough to say in one breath?
Is there exactly one clear turn or reversal in the episode?
Does the episode end before the answer to its open question?
Can a viewer who skipped the previous episode follow it from this episode's first 20 seconds?
Is the episode's duration noted and plausible for the word count?
Are on-screen text cues in the language of the dialogue (Hindi/Hinglish where the series is)?
If AI imagery or voices are planned, is the synthetic-content label noted for the post?
Does the episode move the season's main conflict forward rather than repeating the last episode's beat?
pitfalls: Writing episodes without a season grid: by episode 20 the twists repeat. Draft a one-line-per-episode grid with the turn and cliffhanger of each before scripting.
Monologues and long arguments: vertical close-ups cannot carry them. Break any speech over two lines into an exchange or a reaction shot.
Hinglish that sounds translated ('I am feeling very insulted, Mummy-ji'). Write dialogue the way the characters' city and class actually talk, then read it aloud.
Shock without logic: a twist that contradicts an earlier episode loses binge viewers. Keep a running bible of facts revealed so far.
cards.exemplar_brief: Episode 1 (about 90 seconds) of a fictional 60-episode Hinglish vertical micro-drama 'Contract Wali Biwi' for an Indian micro-drama app: a Gurugram startup founder hires an actress to pose as his wife for his grandmother's 80th birthday in Jaipur. Audience: 18-35 mobile viewers. Deliver: episode header, scenes with headings, dialogue, on-screen text cues and shot sizes; 200-350 words; cold open mid-conflict; ends on a cliffhanger.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C2. Header with duration, characters and the open question; cold open mid-conflict (welcome banner says 'bahu', contract said 'guest'); stakes on a phone screen ('Warna haveli Bua ke naam'); escalation with a power shift (fees double, real family ring); one turn (Dadi calls her by her real name, Naina) and a hard cliffhanger ('Aryan, tu bahar hi ruk'). Scene headings, shot sizes, SUPER cues in the dialogue's Hinglish, one-breath lines, synthetic-content note, ~270 words that fit 90 seconds. Dialogue sounds like the characters, not translated.

cards.name: Mission, vision & values statements
cards.summary: Three short statements: the mission (what the organisation does, for whom, and how), the vision (the future it is working towards), and 3-5 values defined as behaviours. Good ones are specific enough that a staff member can repeat them and use a value to settle a real decision.
use_for: startup culture decks, careers pages and onboarding handbooks
brand refreshes and rebrands where the purpose is restated
schools, colleges, hospitals, NGOs and trusts that publish a vision and mission
family businesses formalising how they work as they hire professional managers
avoid: Values as single nouns with no definition ('Integrity, Excellence, Innovation'): every company has them and nobody can act on them. Define each as a behaviour with a 'this means we...' and a 'we don't...' line.

A mission that is a vision ('To be the world's leading...'): ranking ambitions say nothing about what the team does on Monday. Mission = what we do, for whom, how; vision = the change in the world if we succeed.
Committee sentences that try to include every department's word. Draft from interviews, then cut to one idea per statement.
Values the company does not live: staff notice instantly. Test each value against a real recent decision; if none fits, drop it.

sources.title: Fiverr: Brand Voice & Tone subcategory
sources.supports: page search data on 2026-10-04: num_found 371 gigs; deliverable filter includes Mission & vision statement alongside Brand narrative and Voice & tone guidelines

buyers: startup founders and HR/people teams
branding agencies (as part of a brand platform)
schools, colleges, hospitals and NGOs
family businesses and MSMEs professionalising
cards.value_why: Fiverr lists 'Mission & vision statement' as a deliverable inside its Brand Voice & Tone subcategory (371 gigs on 2026-10-04); it is usually bundled with a brand platform and rarely bought alone.
cards.goal: Staff can repeat the mission from memory and use a value to decide a real trade-off; outsiders understand what the organisation does and why.

structure.does: What we do + for whom + how or why it is different, in words a new hire could say to a relative.
The future state for customers or society if the mission succeeds; concrete enough to picture.
Each: a 1-4 word name in the team's own language; a one-sentence behaviour definition; one 'This means we...' example; one 'We don't...' line that shows the trade-off it costs.
Where the values show up (hiring questions, reviews, product decisions), so they are not decoration.

length.note: Mission and vision are one sentence each; the length comes from the value definitions. Three values well defined beat six labels.

checklist: Is the mission one sentence that names what the organisation does and for whom?
Is the vision a picture of a future state, not a ranking ('No. 1', 'leading')?
Are there 3-5 values, not more?
Does each value have a behaviour definition, not just a noun?
Does each value include a 'we don't' or trade-off line?
Could a competitor paste these statements onto their site unchanged? (Must be no.)
Is every sentence free of buzzwords like world-class, synergy, cutting-edge?
Can the mission be read aloud in under 10 seconds?
pitfalls: Skipping interviews: statements written from a brief alone sound generic. Talk to the founder plus 3-5 staff and collect stories of decisions they are proud of; values come from those stories.
Hindi or regional versions translated word for word. If the team works in Hindi, write the values in Hindi first (or transcreate) so they sound like something people would say.
Aspirational values presented as current fact. If a value is a goal ('We ship weekly'), label it as a commitment.
Changing the statements every year: they lose meaning. Write them to last 3-5 years; update the examples, not the core.
cards.exemplar_brief: Mission, vision and four values for a fictional 45-person Indore logistics startup ('LastMile Malwa') that runs same-day deliveries for kirana stores and D2C brands across Madhya Pradesh, preparing a Series A careers page; audience: current staff and new hires (riders to engineers); English, with each value name also given in Hindi; under 300 words; each value with a 'this means we' and a 'we don't' line.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Mission is one 25-word sentence (what, for whom, why it matters: 'a small shop can keep the promise a big chain makes'); vision is a picture, not a ranking; 4 values each with behaviour line, 'This means we' and a real-cost 'We don't'; Hindi names read naturally (वक़्त का वादा, सीधी बात); usage line ties them to interviews and missed-slot reviews. Not pasteable by a competitor. Nits: the mission names D2C brands but its payoff speaks only to small shops; value 4's example (telling a kirana owner tomorrow's volume will not fit) is slightly abstract.

cards.name: Motivational / inspirational speech
cards.summary: A speech that lifts an audience's energy and commits them to one action, built on a true personal story told with specific detail, a turning point, one lesson, and a direct challenge. Good ones sound like the speaker talking, not like a poster; the audience can retell the story and remembers the one thing they were asked to do.
use_for: annual-day, prize-day and convocation speeches by chief guests and alumni
sales kick-offs, town halls and team rallies
sports team and coaching talks
community, NGO and youth-programme events
avoid: Quote collages (Kalam, Vivekananda, Jobs) stitched together: the audience has heard every one at every annual day. Use one quote at most, and only if the speaker's own story earns it.
Abstract advice ('believe in yourself', 'never give up'). Replace it with the scene where the speaker nearly gave up: the place, the time, what was said.
A story that makes the speaker the hero of everything. Share a failure or a moment someone else helped; audiences trust a speaker who admits a loss.
Ending with 'Thank you' and no ask. End with one concrete action, sized for this audience and this week.

cards.goal: The audience leaves committed to one specific action the speaker named, and can retell the speaker's story.

structure.does: One short protocol line if the event requires it (Indian events usually do), then straight into a scene: a moment, a place, a sound. Or a question this audience is already asking themselves.
The speaker's real difficulty with concrete detail: age, place, what was at stake, what people said. One story, not a CV.
The decision, the person or the small act that changed things. Slow down here; this is the moment the audience will retell.
One idea in one repeatable sentence, said twice (once here, once at the close).
Their version of the struggle: exam pressure, a sales target, a lost match. Name it specifically so they feel seen.
One concrete action with a time frame ('for the next 30 days...'), small enough to start tonight.
Callback to the opening scene or image, the lesson line once more, then thanks.

length.note: Set by the slot: 5 minutes for a chief guest at a school function, 10-15 for a keynote-style rally. Time a read-aloud in the speaker's language and pace before finalising; Hindi and Hinglish delivery speeds differ from English.

checklist: Does the speech reach the first story scene within the first minute?
Does the main story include at least three concrete details (a place, a time, a number, a line someone said)?
Is there a clear turning point the audience could retell?
Is the lesson one sentence, and does it appear at least twice?
Does the speech name the audience's own struggle specifically?
Is there exactly one concrete action with a time frame?
Does the close call back to the opening?
Are borrowed quotes limited to one or none?
Are sentences short enough to say in one breath when read aloud?
pitfalls: Inventing a backstory for the speaker. Interview them (20-30 minutes) for one real story; if they will not share one, build the speech on a true story of someone they know, with permission.
Writing for the eye: long sentences, parentheses, 'as mentioned above'. Read it aloud at speaking pace and cut anything you stumble on.

Wrong language register: an English speech for a Hindi-medium government school audience loses half the room. Ask what language the audience thinks in and write in that, with natural English words where people use them.
Overlong protocol greetings that eat the first two minutes. Agree the minimum salutations with the organiser and keep them to one or two lines.

Natural spoken Hindi with English words, feminine agreement correct throughout, ~930 words for 8 minutes. No borrowed quotes, no cliches.

cards.name: Native ad (Taboola / Outbrain style)
cards.summary: Headline, thumbnail brief and source-name copy for ads that sit in 'recommended for you' widgets on news and content sites and link to an advertorial or landing page. Good native ads earn the click with a specific, honest promise that the landing page keeps; networks reject headlines that exaggerate or do not match the page.
use_for: Taboola, Outbrain and similar recommendation-widget campaigns
driving cold traffic to an advertorial, quiz or long-form landing page
promoting publisher brand-studio content or a D2C story page
headline variant sets for A/B tests on discovery placements
avoid: Classic chumbox bait ('Doctors stunned', 'You won't believe', 'The real reason...'): Outbrain's guidelines tell advertisers to remove sensational words such as 'stuns', 'reveals', 'real reason', 'years later', 'you won't believe'. Promise a specific, true payoff instead.

Headlines the page does not deliver ('12 tips' when there are 40 slides, a 'story' that is a product page). Outbrain asks that headlines align with the content; write the headline last, from the landing page.

Health and money miracle claims (cures, reverses disease, guaranteed returns). Outbrain bars claims to diagnose, cure, prevent or treat disease; ASCI and CCPA rules apply in India. Sell the experience or the mechanism, with evidence.

Hiding that it is an ad. The source name must be the real advertiser, and an advertorial landing page must be labelled 'Advertisement' or 'Advertorial' at the top. India's CCPA 2023 dark-pattern guidelines list disguised advertisement as a dark pattern.

cards.goal: Click the ad and keep reading on the landing page because it delivers what the headline promised.

structure.does: One sentence naming the audience, the curiosity or benefit, and the landing-page section that pays it off. Not published; it keeps every variant honest.

5-10 headlines, each a different angle (how-to, number, question, audience call-out, local hook), each with a specific detail from the landing page. Keep each short enough to show in full in the widget; check the network's current length guidance.
For each 2-3 headlines: the image to use (real product or person in context, readable at small size), no fake before/after, no shocking crops.
The real advertiser name as it should appear under the ad.
One line that adds the second reason to click or names the format ('A 2-minute quiz', '7 photos').
The first screen of the landing page that repeats the headline's promise, plus the 'Advertisement'/'Advertorial' label at the top.

length.note: The whole set: headline variants, thumbnail briefs, description lines and notes. Individual headlines are short; the number of variants drives the total.

checklist: Does every headline promise something the landing page actually delivers?
Does each headline include one specific detail (a number, a place, a product fact, a time)?
Are the variants genuinely different angles rather than reworded copies?
Is every headline free of sensational bait words ('stuns', 'you won't believe', 'real reason', 'doctors hate')?
Is there no claim to cure, treat or prevent a disease, and no guaranteed financial return?
Is the source name the real advertiser?
Does each thumbnail brief describe a real, relevant image (no fake before/after)?
Is the advertorial label ('Advertisement' or 'Advertorial') specified for the top of the landing page?
pitfalls: Optimising for click-through alone: bait headlines win the click and lose the sale (high bounce) and get disapproved. Judge variants on landing-page engagement or conversions, not CTR.
Writing headlines before the landing page exists. Get the page or the advertorial outline first and mine its best facts.
One headline for all sites: a finance-news widget reader and a cricket-site reader need different angles. Write variants per audience or site category.
Ignoring Indian context: 'Bengaluru renters' or a rupee figure beats a generic 'people' or a dollar figure on Indian placements.

cards.name: Video news bulletin / anchor script
cards.summary: The spoken script for a digital or TV news bulletin: opening headlines, anchor links into each story, story reads written for the ear, and bracketed cues for voice-over footage, sound bites, packages, graphics and name supers. Good bulletin copy is understood on one hearing: one idea per sentence, attribution first, numbers rounded, and words that match the pictures on screen.
use_for: Hindi, English and regional digital news bulletins on YouTube, apps and social
TV newsroom rundowns: anchor reads, VO, VO-SOT and package intros
news-in-60-seconds or 'top 5 stories' short bulletins
internal or corporate video news bulletins
avoid: Print sentences read aloud ('The minister, who had earlier said that..., stated...'): listeners lose the subject. Split into two sentences: subject, verb, fact.
Attribution at the end ('...will rise by 20 percent, the RBI said'). On air, put the source first: 'The RBI says...' so the listener knows how much to trust what follows.
Exact figures that cannot be heard (Rs 4,87,63,219). Round for the ear (nearly Rs 4.9 crore) and put the exact number on a full-screen graphic if it matters.
Words that fight the pictures: describing a crowd while the footage shows an empty office. Write VO to the shots listed, or ask for the shot list first.
Sensational anchor adjectives (shocking, sensational, dhamaka). Let the fact carry the weight; it also keeps the bulletin clear of defamation risk.

cards.goal: The viewer understands each story on one hearing and stays through the bulletin to the end.

structure.does: 3-4 top stories, one short line each, written to pictures; newest and most important first.
Anchor name and bulletin, then straight into the lead story's newest fact with the source first.

Each story in a marked form: READER (anchor only), VO (anchor reads over footage, matched to the shot list), VO-SOT (VO then a sound bite, with speaker, in-cue, out-cue and duration), or PKG intro (anchor lead-in, then the reporter's package with its out-cue). One idea per sentence; present tense where accurate.
Cues for name supers (name, designation), locator supers, and full-screen graphics for numbers, quotes or timelines.
'Coming up' line that names a specific later story, before a break or a section change.
Sign-off with where to follow updates, or a one-line recap of the lead story.

length.note: Set by the bulletin's runtime and the number of stories; sound bites and packages take time but few script words. Time the anchor read in the bulletin's language before locking.

checklist: Does each story open with its newest fact, not background?
Does attribution come before the claim ('Police say...', 'पुलिस के मुताबिक...')?
Is every sentence one idea, short enough to read in one breath?
Are large numbers rounded for the ear, with exact figures sent to a graphic where needed?
Is every story marked with its form (READER / VO / VO-SOT / PKG) and every SOT given speaker, in-cue, out-cue and duration?
Are name supers given for every person on screen?
Is the copy free of sensational adjectives and of guilt-assigning words for people who are only accused?
Is there at least one tease that names a specific upcoming story?
If any visual or voice is AI-generated, is a label cue included?
pitfalls: Calling an accused person 'the culprit' or 'the killer' before a court verdict. Use 'accused' and attribute the allegation to police or the complainant.
Abbreviations the ear cannot decode. Say the full name on first use ('the Bihar Public Service Commission'), then the short form.

Hindi bulletin copy that is either translated English or heavy Sanskritised Hindi. Use everyday spoken Hindi as the target channel's anchors speak it; keep English words people actually use (metro, result, cut-off).
Leaving out the out-cue for SOTs and packages: the anchor and the switcher miss the handover. Always write the last words of the bite.

cards.name: News explainer (what we know / why it matters)
cards.summary: An article that makes a current, complicated story understandable: what just happened, the background, how the thing works, who it affects, what is still unknown and what happens next. Good explainers answer the reader's questions in the order they would ask them, use one worked example with real numbers, and separate confirmed facts from open questions.
use_for: 'X explained' pieces on news sites and newsletters
policy, budget, court-ruling and regulation explainers for citizens or customers
brand or fintech editorial explaining a rule change to users (RBI, SEBI, GST updates)
the article version of an explainer reel or YouTube video
avoid: A history lecture first. Lead with what changed this week and why the reader should care; background goes after.
Explaining the mechanism in jargon ('repo rate transmission to EBLR-linked loans'). Explain it as a chain of plain cause and effect, then give the term in brackets.
Mixing confirmed facts with speculation. Use a separate 'What we don't know yet' section and attribute every forecast.
Ending with 'only time will tell'. End with the specific next event: a date, a hearing, a vote, a deadline.
Writing an evergreen guide with a news headline on it. If there is no news peg, write genre:informational_article instead.

cards.goal: The reader can explain the story to someone else in two sentences and knows what to watch for next.

structure.does: Names the news peg and the question answered ('RBI cuts repo rate: what it means for your home-loan EMI'). The dek adds who is affected.
The newest fact, who did it, when, and the one-line reason it matters.
The whole story in bullets for skimmers and for AI answers to lift with attribution.
How we got here: only the history needed to understand today's change.
The mechanism as a plain chain of cause and effect, one analogy at most, and one worked example with real numbers (an EMI, a tax bill, a ticket price).
By group (salaried borrowers, small traders, students), what changes for each and when.
Open questions, disputed claims and pending data, each attributed.
The next dated event, decision or deadline, and what to watch.
Links to the primary documents (notification, judgment, press release, data).

length.note: Shorter when the change is simple and affects one group; longer for budgets, court rulings or multi-party stories. Cut background before cutting the worked example.

checklist: Does the headline name the news peg and the question the piece answers?
Is the newest fact in the first paragraph?
Is there a key-points block of 3-5 bullets near the top?
Is the mechanism explained in plain words, with any technical term defined on first use?
Is there at least one worked example with real numbers relevant to an Indian reader?
Is there a separate section for what is not yet known?
Does it end with the next dated event or decision?
Is every forecast and contested claim attributed to a named source?
Are primary sources linked?
pitfalls: Not updating: explainers on live stories go stale within days. Add an 'Updated on [date]' line and change the 'what we don't know' section as facts land.
Worked examples with invented numbers presented as real. Use the official rate or figure and show the arithmetic; if it is illustrative, say so.
Taking a side in the news voice. Explain each side's argument in its best form and attribute it; opinion belongs in genre:opinion_column.
Explaining for experts. Test the draft on someone outside the field; every question they ask is a missing sentence.

cards.name: News story (hard news article)
cards.summary: A timely, factual report of what happened, written in inverted-pyramid order: the most important fact in the first sentence, then supporting facts in falling importance, every claim attributed to a named source, and no opinion in the writer's voice. Good news stories can be cut from the bottom without losing anything essential.
use_for: breaking and daily news on news sites and hyperlocal apps
trade-publication and business news
corporate newsroom stories written in news style
wire-style copy that other outlets reuse
avoid: A delayed or anecdotal lede on hard news. The first sentence carries who did what, when and where; feature leads belong in genre:feature_article.
Unattributed claims ('The building was illegal'). Attribute every fact that is not self-evident: 'according to the municipal corporation's notice'.
Opinion words in the news voice (shocking, shameful, unfortunately). Report the fact and quote people for the emotion.
One-sided stories about wrongdoing. Seek the response of the person or company accused and report it, or report that they did not respond by publication time.
Rewriting a press release as news without checking. Verify the key fact independently or attribute it clearly to the release.

Is the copy free of opinion words in the writer's voice?

cards.name: News-jacking / trend-reactive post
cards.summary: A fast article or social post that connects a breaking story or viral moment to what the brand actually knows, published while interest is still rising. Good newsjacking adds a useful angle the news coverage lacks (what this means for the brand's customers, and what to do now), gets the facts right, and stays away from tragedy.
use_for: a CA, law or fintech firm explaining a new rule or court ruling to clients within hours
a LinkedIn or X post reacting to an industry announcement with expert commentary
a brand social post riding a viral, light-hearted moment (cricket, a film release, a viral clip)
a newsletter section or blog post that becomes the brand's reference page for a developing story
avoid: Reacting to deaths, disasters, accidents, communal violence or political controversies with brand content. Stay silent or post a plain, respectful message without product mention.

Speed over accuracy: a reaction to a fake viral claim or a misread announcement damages the brand more than missing the moment. Read the primary source (notification, press release, official handle) before writing.
The same 'Congratulations Team India' graphic with a logo that 200 brands post. Add something only this brand can say: its data, its expertise, a specific implication for its customers.
Stretching the link ('This election result reminds us that our sofas...'). If the connection needs explaining, skip the moment.
Writing a full news report. The news is one or two sentences with a link; the post's value is the angle and the advice.

sources.title: Elevate Network: Top Meme Marketing Trends in India 2026
sources.supports: Indian meme-marketing agency describing paid brand campaigns run through networks of meme pages, increasingly in Hindi and regional languages (vendor source, low confidence)

buyers: B2B firms whose clients are hit by rule changes (CA, law, fintech, HR-tech)
D2C and consumer brands with an always-on social team
PR agencies offering rapid expert commentary
social media and meme-marketing agencies
cards.value_why: Indian brands buy moment marketing through meme and social agencies (Elevate Network, a vendor source); the article and LinkedIn form is usually part of a content retainer rather than a separate marketplace category.
cards.goal: The reader sees the brand as the most useful voice on the moment and takes the next step (reads the guide, books a call, shares or follows).

structure.does: What happened, when, and the primary source link or name. Facts only.
What this means for this brand's audience specifically; the reason this brand is qualified to say it.
3-5 concrete implications or steps: who is affected, from when, what to do now, a number or example. For a light social moment, this is the joke or the brand's twist instead.
One natural line connecting to the product, service or expertise, if the moment allows it.
Low-friction next step: read the full guide, save the post, DM a keyword, book a short call.
'As of [time, date]' and a line saying it will be updated, for stories still developing.

length.note: A social reaction is 60-250 words; a blog or newsletter version runs 400-900. Ship the short version first while the topic is rising, then expand it into the reference article.

checklist: Does the post state the news in one or two sentences with its source named or linked?
Is the angle specific to this brand's audience and expertise?
Does it give at least one concrete implication or action (date, amount, who is affected)?
Is the topic free of tragedy, death, disaster and communal or partisan conflict?
Is every fact checked against the primary source rather than a forward or screenshot?
Is the brand mention one line or less, and natural?
Is there a single low-friction CTA?
Is there a timestamp or 'as of' line if the story is still developing?
pitfalls: Waiting for three approval rounds: the moment passes. Agree a fast-lane approval rule in advance (who signs off in under an hour, which topics are off-limits).
Using news photos, match footage or film stills you do not have rights to. Use your own graphics, text posts or licensed images.
Election periods: brand or issue content that touches parties or candidates can fall under election-period rules. Keep brand newsjacking non-partisan.
Never updating: a reaction post that stays wrong after the rule is clarified keeps getting shared. Edit it with an 'Updated' note or take it down.

require.label: names or links the news source

ban.label: filler openers
ban.regex: (?i)as we all know|in today'?s fast-paced world|needless to say|big news,? guys

cards.exemplar_brief: LinkedIn post by a fictional Pune CA firm ('Kulkarni & Rao Associates') reacting within hours to this supplied decision (demo facts): the GST Council met on Saturday 3 October 2026 and cut the GST rate on stainless-steel water bottles and flasks (HSN 7323) from 18% to 5%, effective Thursday 22 October 2026; notification no. 12/2026-Central Tax (Rate) dated Monday 5 October 2026; source: GST Council press release, 3 October 2026. Worked example the post may use: a bottle with an MRP of Rs 999 inclusive of GST has a base price of about Rs 847 at 18%; at 5% the same base price gives about Rs 889. Audience: D2C founders with Rs 1-20 crore revenue; English; 150-250 words; names the source, gives 3 practical implications (pricing, invoices, stock already shipped), marks any figure not supplied as [verify], ends with a CTA to a free 15-minute call.

verified.note: ROUND 2: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Peg, source and notification in two sentences, an angle for steel-bottle D2C brands, the three implications the brief asked for (pricing with the supplied Rs 847 / Rs 889 example, billing and marketplace tax settings, stock already shipped under s.14), the s.171 pass-on duty flagged, a one-line brand tie, a single 15-minute-call CTA and an as-of line; dates and weekdays correct; 246 words, 2 hashtags. Round 1's s.12 error is fixed. Nits (writer): five [verify] tags must be cleared before posting; 'Hold the MRP instead and you keep the extra margin' presents non-compliance as an option before the s.171 caveat. | round 1: weak 7

cards.name: Novel / novel chapter (long-form fiction)
cards.summary: Book-length fiction delivered chapter by chapter. A good chapter has a point-of-view character who wants something now, a scene where that want meets resistance, a change by the end (a reveal, a decision, a loss), and a final paragraph that gives the reader a reason to turn the page.
use_for: ghostwritten novels for authors and personalities
self-published fiction on Kindle and other e-book stores
sample chapters sent to literary agents and publishers with a query letter and synopsis
Hindi upanyas and bilingual fiction projects
avoid: Opening with backstory, weather or a character waking up. Start in a scene where the character is already under pressure; feed backstory in later, a line at a time.
Chapters where nothing changes. Before writing, state in one line what is different at the end of the chapter; if nothing is, merge it.
Head-hopping: switching whose thoughts we hear inside a scene. Keep one point-of-view character per scene; change POV only at a scene break.
Summarising the big moments ('They argued for hours'). Dramatise the key moments in scene with dialogue and action; summarise the connecting tissue.
Ending chapters with the character going to sleep or everything resolved. End on a question, a decision pending or a new threat.

sources.title: Reedsy: Find Book Ghostwriting Services
sources.supports: marketplace guide prices: book ghostwriting average $450 per 1,000 words (2,006 offers, 2025); book proposal $750-$10,000

buyers: authors and public personalities hiring ghostwriters
self-publishers on Amazon KDP
book packagers and small publishers
serial fiction and audio-story platforms
cards.value_why: Reedsy's ghostwriting marketplace reports an average of $450 per 1,000 words for book ghostwriting (2,006 offers, 2025), so a full novel is a substantial commission even though most chapters are written by the author.
cards.goal: The reader finishes the chapter and starts the next one.

structure.does: POV character, what they want in this chapter, what stands in the way, what changes by the end, and the chapter's closing hook. Not published.
Drop the reader into a scene: a character, a place, a want and a pressure, with a concrete sensory detail in the first paragraph.
Goal, conflict, outcome: the character tries, meets resistance (a person, a fact, themselves) and ends worse off or changed. Dialogue carries conflict and subtext.
The character absorbs what happened and makes a decision; short, interior, it sets the next want.
The reveal, reversal or decision that makes the situation different from the chapter's start.
The last paragraph or line opens a question, a danger or a decision for the next chapter.

length.note: Per chapter. Genre sets the rhythm: thrillers run short, fast chapters; literary and fantasy run longer. Total manuscript length expectations differ by category; the agent's, publisher's or platform's guidelines own those numbers.

checklist: Does the chapter open inside a scene rather than with backstory or setting description?
Is there one point-of-view character per scene?
Does the POV character want something specific in this chapter?
Is the key moment dramatised in scene with dialogue and action rather than summarised?
Is the situation at the end of the chapter different from the start?
Does the last paragraph give a reason to read the next chapter?
Are names, timeline and facts consistent with earlier chapters and the series bible?
Does the dialogue sound like these characters (age, region, class), read aloud?
Is the prose free of stock phrases ('little did she know', 'a shiver ran down his spine')?
pitfalls: Writing without an outline or bible: by chapter 15 a character's eye colour, a date or a rule of the world contradicts chapter 3. Keep a running bible of facts and update it after every chapter.
Ghostwriting in your own voice instead of the author's. Read the author's existing writing or record them telling stories, and match their rhythm and vocabulary.
Hindi and Hinglish dialogue in an English novel transliterated inconsistently. Pick one spelling scheme (e.g. 'nahi' vs 'nahin') and record it in the style sheet.

Relying on AI-generated passages for a manuscript whose rights the client needs to own and register: copyright protection for AI-generated material is limited in the US. Disclose your process to the client and keep human authorship substantive.

ban.label: stock fiction phrases
ban.regex: (?i)little did (he|she|they|i) know|a shiver ran down (his|her|my|their) spine|it was all (just )?a dream|let out a breath (he|she|they|i) didn'?t know

cards.exemplar_brief: Chapter 1 of a fictional English-language crime novel set in Varanasi: Meera, a 34-year-old woman who runs her late father's boat on the ghats, finds a foreign tourist's passport and a blood-stained ticket stub in her boat at dawn and must decide whether to go to the police, who already distrust her family. Close third-person POV; natural Hindi words in dialogue; 2,000-2,800 words; opens in scene; ends on a hook.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Opens inside a scene with a concrete wrong detail (the knot), close third on Meera throughout, a clear want and pressure, the find dramatised, dialogue that carries conflict and class (Lakhan, Bhola, the constable), the family history with the thana folded in rather than front-loaded, a reveal (her dead father's name and boat number on the slip, dated the week the ledger vanished) and a strong closing turn (her first lie to a policeman). Consistent 'nahi/kuch/thana' spelling. Nits: Bhola's 'wo nao tumhari nao ke paas rukhi nahi' contradicts the premise that someone used her boat; 'rukhi' and 'Hass' are misspellings (ruki, Hans); the bailing line ('never lifting the can above the gunwale so the water fell back in') reads backwards.

cards.name: Obituary
cards.summary: A news-feature published after a death: it confirms the facts of the death like news (who, age, when, where, cause only if confirmed), then explains what the person did and why they mattered through specific anecdotes and quotes. Good obituaries are accurate, specific and fair, including the complications of a public life, not just praise.
use_for: obituaries of public figures, artists, sportspeople and business leaders for news outlets
trade and industry publications marking the death of a leader in the field
institutional obituaries for universities, companies and associations
prepared (advance) obituaries newsrooms keep on file for prominent people
avoid: Publishing before the death is confirmed by family or an official source. Name who confirmed it in the story.
Speculating about the cause of death. Report a cause only when the family or an official source states it, and attribute it.
A CV in prose (born, studied, joined, retired). Pick the 2-3 things that made this life matter and tell them with scenes and quotes.
Condolence-message cliches ('irreparable loss', 'a void that can never be filled', 'end of an era'). Let a specific detail or a colleague's quote carry the feeling.
Leaving out what everyone knows for a public figure (a scandal, a conviction, a famous failure). Mention it fairly and in proportion; omitting it costs the piece its credibility.

sources.title: Jasmine Roberts, Introduction to Journalism I (NVCC Pressbooks, CC BY-NC 4.0, 2023): Types of news stories
sources.supports: news stories are taught by type: straight news uses the inverted pyramid, features use storytelling devices

buyers: newspapers and digital news outlets
trade, industry and professional publications
universities, companies and associations (in-memoriam pieces)
families commissioning a tribute article for publication
cards.value_why: Written mostly by staff journalists; journalism courses treat it as a hybrid of news and feature, and no freelance marketplace category was found on 2026-10-04.
cards.goal: Readers learn the confirmed facts of the death and understand who the person was and why their life mattered.

structure.does: Name, what they are known for, and the death, with age if known ('Ustad X, who took Bhojpuri folk to Doordarshan, dies at 84').
Name, the identity tag that explains why they matter, died, when, where, age.
Who confirmed the death; the cause only if confirmed and stated by family or an official.
The nut paragraph: the 1-2 achievements or qualities the obituary will prove.
Highlights in order or by theme, each told with a specific anecdote, a number or a quote from family, colleagues or the person's own past interviews (credited).
For public figures: disputes, failures or controversies, stated fairly and in proportion.
Family members as the family wishes them listed; funeral or prayer-meeting details if public.
A quote or anecdote that captures the person; not a summary.

length.note: Driven by the person's prominence and by how much verified material exists. A trade-publication obituary may be 300-500 words; a major public figure runs long.

checklist: Is the death confirmed, and does the story say who confirmed it?
Does the lede give name, why they matter, the death, date or day, place and age?
Is any cause of death attributed to family or an official source (or left out)?
Is there a clear paragraph on why this person mattered?
Does the life story use at least two specific anecdotes or quotes rather than a list of positions held?
For a public figure, are known controversies mentioned fairly?
Are names, dates, titles and spellings checked with the family or records?
Is it free of condolence cliches?
pitfalls: Relying on Wikipedia or a single old profile for dates and titles: errors in obituaries hurt families and get repeated. Check birth year, positions and awards with the family or primary records.
Calling the family for quotes without care. Introduce yourself, explain the piece, ask what they would like people to know, and accept a no.
Inflated titles and awards family members add in grief ('world-famous', 'first ever'). Verify 'first' and 'only' claims or drop them.
Quoting social-media tributes as if they were interviews. Credit them as posts, and prefer people who actually knew the person.

ban.label: condolence cliches
ban.regex: (?i)void that can never be filled|irreparable loss|end of an era|अपूरणीय क्षति

cards.exemplar_brief: Obituary for a fictional Patna tabla maestro, Pandit Ramashray Mishra, for a Bihar culture news site, written from this fact sheet (demo facts); English; 600-900 words; any detail not in the fact sheet marked [verify]. Identity tag: Patna tabla maestro and teacher. Died Tuesday 6 October 2026 at his home in Kankarbagh, Patna, aged 84 (born 1942 in Laheriasarai, Darbhanga); death confirmed by his son Anand Mishra, a school teacher; cause: age-related illness, per the family. Trained from age 9 under Pandit Shivnath Jha (demo name) in the Banaras gharana. Career: joined All India Radio Patna as a staff tabla accompanist in 1966 and stayed until 2002; toured 12 cities accompanying the vocalist Vidushi Sarita Devi in 1984; founded the Laya Kendra in Patna in 1989, teaching over 200 students, free for children from poor families. Colleague quotes: Sarita Devi, Hindustani vocalist: 'He never played over the singer. He listened, and then the tabla answered.' Arvind Kumar, sarangi player and former AIR colleague: 'He would rehearse the same sixteen beats for an hour until the room breathed with it.' Dr Meena Sinha, principal of a Patna music college: 'Half the tabla teachers in Bihar sat on his floor first.' Dispute: in 1994 the state music academy withdrew an announced Rs 1 lakh senior fellowship after he criticised its selection in a newspaper letter; the academy said the committee lacked quorum and the list was under review; he said it was punishment for the letter; in 1997 a new committee reinstated the fellowship and he accepted it, giving the money to the Laya Kendra. Survivors: son Anand and daughter Mala Jha, four grandchildren; his wife Kamla Devi died in 2015. Cremation on Wednesday 7 October at Gulbi Ghat, Patna.

verified.note: ROUND 2: P2 S2 Sp2 V1 C1. All supplied facts used correctly: a full lede (AIR Patna, 36 years, 1966-2002), the son's confirmation and the family's stated cause, a real 'why he mattered' paragraph (playing behind a singer, and teaching), all three quotes placed well, the 1994-97 fellowship dispute with both sides and how it ended, survivors and rites, a quote close; 605 words. Nits (writer): it again leans on a stock line ('His life was not without a public dispute'); [verify] tags are put on facts the sheet supplies ('source of the figure' for the 200 students) and 'Reporting gap' notes sit inside the copy; the timeline box repeats the body. | round 1: weak 6

cards.name: Obituary / death notice
cards.summary: A short published notice of a death, in a newspaper, on social media or on WhatsApp, giving the person's name and identity, age, date of death, the family, and the date, time and venue of the funeral or prayer meeting. Good notices are accurate to the last digit of the time, dignified, short, and written in the family's own religious and cultural register.
use_for: newspaper classified death notices and shraddhanjali ads
prayer-meeting, uthala, chautha, tehrvi, rasm pagdi or memorial-service notices
WhatsApp and Facebook announcements to relatives and community groups
company, RWA or association notices of a member's or employee's death; first death-anniversary remembrance ads
avoid: Any error in name, date, day, time or venue: people arrive at the wrong place on the wrong day. Read every detail back to the family before release, and check that the weekday matches the date.
Long flowery text. The reader needs who, when and where; a line or two of feeling is enough.

Religious phrases from the wrong tradition. Match the family: 'Om Shanti' or 'heavenly abode' for many Hindu families, 'Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un' for Muslim families, 'called to eternal rest' for Christian families, and ask when unsure.
Stating the cause of death unless the family asks for it.
buyers: families (directly or through newspaper ad desks and agents)
funeral and last-rites service providers
companies, RWAs, schools and community associations
cards.value_why: Written by families and newspaper classified desks; little freelance market, though funeral-service providers and ad agents draft them as part of their service.
cards.goal: Everyone who knew the person learns of the death and knows exactly when and where to attend the funeral or prayer meeting.

structure.does: A short formula of grief in the family's register ('With deep sorrow we inform...', 'अत्यंत दुःख के साथ सूचित किया जाता है...').
Full name with honorific as the family uses it, age, and one identity tag (wife of, retired principal of, founder of).
Date (and day), city; a tradition-appropriate phrase if the family wants one.
Type of ceremony, date, weekday, time (with AM/PM or 'subah/shaam'), venue with a landmark.
Grieving family members in the order the family gives (spouse, children, grandchildren), then 'and the entire [surname] family'.
One or two phone numbers if the family wants calls; photo caption line for print.

length.note: Newspaper notices are usually priced by size, so families keep them short; a WhatsApp version can carry the venue map link. Remembrance and anniversary ads are similar length.

checklist: Is the name spelled exactly as the family confirmed, with the honorific they use?
Are age and date of death given?
Does the ceremony line give type, date, weekday, time and venue with a landmark?
Does the weekday match the date?
Are family names in the order the family gave?
Is the religious or cultural phrasing right for this family's tradition?
Is the cause of death left out unless the family asked for it?
Is it free of emoji and exclamation marks?
pitfalls: Copying a template from another family's notice and leaving a name or date from the old one. Write fresh from the details sheet and read it back aloud.
Mixing scripts in the newspaper version (a Hindi notice with the venue in English abbreviations). Write the whole notice in one script; numbers can stay as numerals.
Forgetting the time format: '4 o'clock' leaves AM/PM unclear. Write '4:00 PM' or 'शाम 4 बजे'.
Adding every relative and causing offence by omission. Ask the family for the final list and the order.
cards.exemplar_brief: Newspaper death notice and a WhatsApp version for a fictional Kanpur family: Smt. Kamla Devi Agarwal, 78, retired Hindi teacher, died on Sunday 4 October 2026 in Kanpur. Uthavna (prayer meeting): Wednesday 7 October 2026, 4:00 to 5:00 pm, Agrasen Bhawan, Swaroop Nagar, Kanpur, near Swaroop Nagar Market. Family, in the order the family gave: husband Shri Om Prakash Agarwal; sons Rajeev Agarwal and Sanjeev Agarwal; daughters-in-law Neelam Agarwal and Rekha Agarwal; daughter Sunita Gupta and son-in-law Ashok Gupta; grandchildren Aarav, Ishita and Kabir; and the entire Agarwal family. Contact: 98765 43210 (demo). Hindi in Devanagari; newspaper version 60-100 words; WhatsApp version 50-90 words with a line for the venue map link; no emoji.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp1 V2 C1. Right register for a Hindu Agarwal family: 'अत्यंत दुःख के साथ सूचित किया जाता है', name with Smt., age, identity tag (सेवानिवृत्त हिंदी शिक्षिका), ceremony line with type/weekday/date/time-with-'बजे'/venue/landmark, family order slot then 'एवं समस्त अग्रवाल परिवार', contact, WhatsApp version with forward request and map-link line; one script, no emoji, no cause. Flat but correct; a 'पूज्य माताजी' style warmth line would lift it. Card fault: the brief says date, uthavna time, venue and family list are 'supplied' but gives none, so every detail is a placeholder. CARD FIX: exemplar_brief -> supply date and weekday of death, uthavna date/time/venue with landmark, family list in order and a phone number. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_b): exemplar_brief now supplies the date and weekday of death, uthavna date/time/venue with landmark, the ordered family list and a phone number; re-judge pending.

cards.name: Offer stack / offer page
cards.summary: The part of a sales page, VSL or webinar pitch that lays out exactly what the buyer gets: the core product, each bonus and the job it does, the guarantee, the price against a real anchor, payment options and any real deadline, then a recap of the whole stack. Good offer stacks make the deal easy to understand and every value claim true; each bonus removes an obstacle rather than padding the list.
use_for: the offer section of a long-form sales page or VSL
the closing slides and script of a webinar or masterclass pitch
course, cohort, coaching and membership launches
D2C bundles and SaaS annual-plan offers
avoid: Inflated 'total value' figures ('Worth Rs 99,999!') for items never sold at that price. State standalone prices only for things actually sold separately; otherwise describe what the bonus saves the buyer.

Countdown timers that reset and 'only 3 seats left' claims not tied to real capacity: false urgency is a listed dark pattern in India's CCPA 2023 guidelines. Use a real cohort start date or a real cap and say why it exists.
Revealing fees (GST, platform charges, shipping) only at checkout: drip pricing is also a listed dark pattern. Show the full price, including taxes, in the stack.
Bonus padding (ten PDFs nobody reads). Keep 2-4 bonuses, each tied to an objection or a faster result.
Vague guarantees ('100% satisfaction'). State the days, the condition and how to claim.

sources.title: CCPA Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023 (gazette PDF)
sources.supports: false urgency (fake scarcity or popularity) and drip pricing are listed dark patterns in Annexure 1

buyers: course creators, coaches and cohort-based educators
info-product and webinar marketers
D2C brands building bundles and launch offers
SaaS teams designing annual or launch plans
cards.value_why: Usually written as a section of a sales page, VSL or webinar pitch rather than bought alone; no marketplace lists it as a separate deliverable.
cards.goal: The buyer sees clearly what they get, believes it is worth more than the price, feels the risk is removed, and buys or enrols.

structure.does: Names the offer and the core outcome in the buyer's words.
What it is, format, duration, access period, and 3-6 outcome-led bullets (what the buyer can do after).
2-4 bonuses, each: name, what it is, and the obstacle or objection it removes ('No time to set up? We build your first...'). Standalone price only if genuinely sold separately.
The real alternative cost (hiring a consultant, a competitor's plan, the cost of the problem), then the price with taxes, and payment options (UPI, EMI, cards).
Exact terms: number of days, what qualifies, how to claim, how fast the refund lands.
Only if true: cohort start date, seat cap with its reason (live Q&A capacity), launch-price end date.
Everything listed once more in a short list, then the price.
Button text with the action and the price ('Enrol for Rs 14,999'), plus one reassurance line (secure payment, refund terms).

length.note: Higher prices and colder audiences need more explanation of each item and the guarantee; a warm-list offer for a low-priced product can sit at the short end.

checklist: Does the core product section say what it is, its format, duration and access period?
Does each bonus name the obstacle or objection it removes?
Are standalone prices stated only for items actually sold separately?
Is the full price, including taxes, shown before the CTA?
Are payment options stated?
Does the guarantee give days, conditions and how to claim?
Is every deadline or scarcity claim real and explained?
Is there a recap list of everything in the offer?
Does the CTA button name the action and the price?
For courses and coaching, are results claims free of guarantees of jobs, ranks or income?
pitfalls: Writing the stack before the product is fixed: bonuses get promised that the team cannot deliver. Confirm each item and its delivery date with the client before writing.

Course and coaching ads with success claims (selection rates, ranks, salary hikes) that cannot be substantiated: India's CCPA has separate coaching-sector advertising guidelines. Use verifiable student outcomes with consent, or none.
Too many tiers: three plans plus four add-ons stall the decision. One offer, or two tiers with a clear recommended one.
Copying a US-style stack for Indian buyers: dollar-style anchors and 'one payment of 997' read foreign. Use rupee figures, GST-inclusive prices and UPI or EMI options.

require.label: states a guarantee or refund term

ban.label: hype urgency
ban.regex: (?i)\b(act now|last chance ever|never again|once in a lifetime|price doubles at midnight)\b

cards.exemplar_brief: Offer section of the sales page for a fictional 6-week live cohort 'GST for D2C Founders' run by a Jaipur CA: Rs 14,999 including GST in one payment, or 3 monthly UPI payments of Rs 5,000 (Rs 15,000 in total: the extra Re 1 is rounding, there is no EMI convenience fee); 40 seats capped by live Q&A capacity; cohort starts Saturday 7 November 2026 and enrolment closes Wednesday 4 November or when the 40 seats fill; 7-day refund after the first class (request by Saturday 14 November). Audience: D2C founders with Rs 1-10 crore revenue. English with a light Hinglish line; 400-600 words; 3 bonuses each tied to an objection; a real anchor (the cost of hiring a consultant to answer one GST notice, marked [verify]); stack recap; CTA with price.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Headline names offer and outcome; core product with format, weekly live class, recording-access slot and 5 outcome bullets; 3 bonuses each opened by the objection it removes, no fake standalone prices; anchor to a consultant's notice fee [verify]; GST-inclusive price, UPI/card/EMI; guarantee with days, condition, how to claim and refund route; real seat cap with its reason; recap; CTA 'Enrol for Rs 14,999' plus reassurance; no result promises; natural Hinglish line. Writer handled the EMI gap honestly (Rs 15,600, Rs 601 more). Nits: headline 'handle your own GST notices and returns' overpromises against the bullet 'know when to hand it to your CA'; bonus 1 (template pack) answers 'no time' only loosely. CARD FIX: exemplar_brief -> make the EMI reconcile (3 x Rs 5,000) or state the EMI convenience fee, so the numbers agree with 'Rs 14,999 including GST'. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_b): exemplar_brief now makes the EMI reconcile (3 x Rs 5,000 = Rs 15,000, Re 1 rounding, no convenience fee) and supplies the start, enrolment-close and refund dates; re-judge pending.

cards.name: Strategy / OKR document
cards.summary: A plan that says where an organisation is going, the choice it is making to get there, and how progress will be measured: a diagnosis of the situation, a guiding choice with explicit trade-offs, a few objectives, and 3-5 measurable key results under each. Good strategy documents are written as reasoned narrative, separate outcomes (key results) from tasks (initiatives), and name an owner for every result.
use_for: annual and quarterly OKRs for startups and teams
strategy memos for leadership offsites and board discussions
narrative decision memos (the 'six-pager' style) read before a meeting
department, NGO or programme annual plans
avoid: Key results that are tasks ('Launch the new website', 'Hire 3 SDRs'). Write the outcome the task should move, with baseline and target: 'Raise website demo requests from 40 to 90 a month by 30 June'. Put the task under initiatives.
A goal dressed up as strategy ('Grow revenue 3x'). State the choice that will get there and what the team will stop doing to afford it.
Ten objectives. A team that has ten priorities has none; keep a few objectives and cut or park the rest in a 'not this quarter' list.
Bullet-only decks for decisions that need reasoning. Write the diagnosis and the choice as paragraphs; bullets hide missing logic.
Unmeasurable KRs ('Improve customer happiness'). Name the metric, the source and the date.
