cards.goal: Leadership agrees on the few priorities and the choice behind them, and every team knows the measurable results it owns and by when.

structure.does: The situation, the choice and the top 3 results in one paragraph a busy reader can stop after.
What is going on and the one or two critical challenges, with data (revenue, churn, market, competition).
The approach chosen, why it beats the alternatives considered, and an explicit 'we will not' list.
A few qualitative, concrete, action-oriented statements of what must be achieved this period.
3-5 per objective: metric, baseline, target, date, owner, data source.
The projects expected to move each KR, with owner and timing; clearly separate from KRs.
What could block the plan, what is needed from other teams, and early warning signs.
When KRs are checked and scored, by whom, and what triggers a change of plan.

length.note: A team's quarterly OKR sheet with a short rationale is the low end; a company strategy memo with diagnosis and alternatives runs long. Data tables go in an appendix and do not count.

checklist: Does the document open with a summary of situation, choice and top results?
Does the diagnosis name the critical challenge with data?
Does it state the choice made and at least one explicit 'we will not' item?
Are objectives few and written as concrete outcomes, not slogans?
Does every key result have a metric, baseline, target and date?
Does every key result have one named owner?
Are initiatives (tasks) listed separately from key results?
Are risks and dependencies stated?
Is the review cadence stated?
pitfalls: Sandbagging or fantasy targets: KRs everyone will hit, or ones nobody believes. Set targets from the baseline and stated capacity, and say in the doc whether OKRs are stretch or committed.
Copying last year's OKRs with new numbers. Start from a fresh diagnosis; if the challenge changed, the objectives change.
Metrics nobody can measure today. Check each KR's data source exists before the quarter starts, or make 'set up tracking for X' an initiative.
Jargon from strategy books ('north star', 'flywheel', 'synergies') without saying what they mean here. Translate each into the plain change the team will see.
cards.exemplar_brief: Quarterly strategy and OKR memo for a fictional 30-person Kochi SaaS that sells appointment booking to clinics; supplied data: monthly churn about 6% among single-doctor clinics, 60% of new signups from WhatsApp referrals, two sales hires leaving. English; 900-1,400 words; summary, diagnosis, guiding choice with a 'we will not' list, 3 objectives with 3-4 key results each (baseline, target, date, owner), initiatives listed separately, risks, review cadence.

Summary a reader can stop after; diagnosis uses the supplied data and derives the ~48% one-year survival correctly; guiding choice with alternatives A/B/C and a concrete 'we will not' list; 3 outcome objectives; 3 KRs each with baseline, target, date, owner and data source (unknown baselines as slots, churn cause stated as unknown); initiatives separate from KRs; risks with an early-warning threshold; review cadence with stretch vs committed scoring and a change trigger. cards.name: In-product onboarding flow copy
cards.summary: The copy a new user sees in their first session: welcome screen, setup steps, permission requests, tooltips, checklist, empty states and the first success message. Good onboarding gets the user to the first useful result fast: one job per screen, buttons that say what happens, progress shown, optional steps skippable, and every permission asked in context with its reason.
use_for: first-run screens for Android and iOS apps
setup wizards and getting-started checklists in SaaS dashboards
product tours, tooltips and coach marks
permission primers (notifications, contacts, location) and KYC or verification steps in fintech apps
avoid: A carousel of 4-5 feature slides before the user can do anything. Skip the tour; put the first real action on screen one and teach features when they are needed.
Asking for every permission at launch. Ask at the moment it matters, after a one-line primer saying what the user gets ('Allow notifications so we can tell you when a customer pays').
Generic buttons ('Next', 'Continue', 'Submit') on every screen. Label with the action and object: 'Add first customer', 'Send reminder'.
Confirm-shaming decline links ('No thanks, I like losing money'): confirm shaming is a listed dark pattern in India's CCPA 2023 guidelines. Use a neutral 'Not now' or 'Skip'.
Long forms upfront. Ask only what is needed for the first result; collect the rest later.

cards.goal: The new user completes the first meaningful action (their first useful result) in the first session.

structure.does: Headline naming the outcome the user came for, one supporting line, primary button for the first step, secondary for sign-in.
1-3 questions that change what the user sees next (language, role, goal), with a line on why you ask.
One job per screen: title as an action, one helper line, clear field labels, button with verb + object, progress ('Step 2 of 3'), skip where the step is optional.
Before the system dialog: what the user gets and when it is used; buttons 'Allow' and 'Not now'.
Empty state or template that makes the first action obvious, with one CTA.
Confirms what just happened in plain words and offers the next step.
3-5 getting-started items and tooltips that appear on the feature they explain; each tooltip says what it does and why it helps.
Messages for failed verification, no internet, wrong OTP: what happened, how to fix it.

length.note: Total across all screens. More steps are not better; the length comes from the number of screens the product truly needs before first value, plus the error states.

checklist: Can the user start a real action from the first screen?
Does each screen have exactly one job?
Does every primary button name the action (verb + object) rather than 'Next' or 'Submit'?
Is progress shown in multi-step setup?
Are optional steps skippable, with a neutral 'Skip' or 'Not now'?
Is every permission request preceded by a primer that says what the user gets?
Is there a success message after the first key action?
Do error states say what went wrong and how to fix it, without blaming the user?
Is the language the user chose used consistently, with the same term for the same thing on every screen?
Is every decline option free of shaming or guilt?
pitfalls: Writing screens in isolation. Lay all screens out in order (a table: screen, title, body, buttons, state) and read the flow start to finish as a new user.

Hindi or regional versions translated from English UI. Write or transcreate for how users talk ('udhaar', 'paise bhejo'), keep familiar English words (UPI, OTP, WhatsApp), and test on the smallest phone screen for overflow.
Consent buried in a setup step. Personal-data consent needs its own clear notice and an affirmative action; pre-ticked boxes do not count.
Never measuring. Name the activation metric (e.g. first reminder sent) the copy is meant to move, so variants can be tested.
cards.exemplar_brief: First-run onboarding copy for a fictional Android app 'KhataSaathi' that helps kirana shop owners in Uttar Pradesh record udhaar (credit) and send WhatsApp payment reminders. Screens: welcome, language choice, shop name, add first customer, contacts permission primer, first reminder (first-value moment), success message, 4-item getting-started checklist, wrong-OTP error. Hindi in Devanagari with everyday English words (UPI, WhatsApp, OTP); 150-300 words total; laid out as a screen-by-screen table.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Screen-by-screen table covering all 9 requested screens; one job per screen, verb+object buttons (नाम सेव करें, ग्राहक जोड़ें, WhatsApp पर भेजें), Step 1/3-3/3 progress, contacts primer before the system dialog with a neutral 'अभी नहीं', first-value reminder preview, success, 4-item checklist, non-blaming OTP error; everyday Hindi with UPI/WhatsApp/OTP; consistent udhaar/grahak/reminder terms; 237 words. Writer faults: the success screen promises 'रामलाल जी का जवाब आते ही यहाँ दिखेगा', which an app that hands off to WhatsApp cannot see, and 'रिमाइंडर भेज दिया गया' cannot be confirmed either; the OTP error says 'नंबर' where it means the OTP; 'आप किस भाषा में चलाएँगे?' drops its object (ऐप).

cards.name: One-pager / sell sheet
cards.summary: A single page that sums up a product or service for a buyer: who it is for, the problem, how it works, the proof, and one next step with contact details. Good one-pagers are scannable, specific (numbers, named customers, certifications), written for the person who will be forwarded the PDF, and end with one clear action.
use_for: sales leave-behinds and follow-up email attachments
the page a champion forwards to their boss or procurement
trade-show and exhibition handouts
product datasheets and capability statements for tenders and partners
avoid: Cramming every feature into 9pt type. Pick the three benefits this buyer cares about and cut the rest; link to the full spec.
Generic claims ('innovative', 'world-class quality'). Replace with a number, a named customer, a certification or a test result.
No next step, or five next steps. End with one action (book a demo, request a quote, start a trial) and a named contact.
One version for every buyer. A plant head and a CFO need different first lines; make a version per main segment.

cards.goal: The reader, or the boss they forward it to, understands what is offered and takes the one next step (book a demo, call, request a quote).

structure.does: Logo, product name and a one-line value proposition: for whom and the outcome.
The buyer's problem in their language, with a number if one is available.
Three steps or 3-5 short bullets describing the solution in plain words.
Three benefits, each a bold headline plus one proof line (metric, customer, standard).
One case snippet with a number, customer logos, certifications or a named testimonial.
Short spec table for products, or pricing hint and engagement model for services.
One action, a named person, phone or WhatsApp, email, URL or QR code.

length.note: One printed side. Technical datasheets with spec tables can run longer in the table; the prose stays short.

checklist: Does the header say who it is for and the outcome in one line?
Is the problem stated in the buyer's language?
Is 'how it works' three steps or a few bullets, without jargon?
Are there exactly three main benefits, each with a proof line?
Is there at least one specific proof (number, named customer, certification)?
Is there exactly one call to action with a named contact?
Does the copy fit one printed side at a readable size?
Are claims like 'best', 'No. 1' or percentages substantiated or removed?
pitfalls: Writing it like a brochure about the company's history. The buyer cares about their problem; company background gets one line at most.
Numbers without context ('30% savings'). Say compared with what, for whom and over what period.
Ignoring how it travels: it is usually a PDF on WhatsApp or email. Put the product name and contact in the file name and on the page, and make sure it reads on a phone screen.
Unapproved customer logos and quotes. Get written permission before naming a customer.

Customer result to use (approved, mill anonymised): a 25,000-spindle cotton spinning mill near Tiruppur cut energy use per kg of yarn from 3.42 to 3.15 kWh/kg (about 8%) in 90 days after the meters showed compressor idle load, and its power-factor penalty fell from Rs 1.8 lakh to Rs 0.2 lakh a month. Contact: Meenakshi Subramanian, solutions manager, WhatsApp +91 90000 00002 (demo), meenakshi@loomwatt.example.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp1 V2 C1. Scannable and in card order: one-line value header, problem in the plant head's language ('by the time the bill arrives, the month is over'), 3-step how it works with mill sections named, 3 benefits with proof lines, case slot, offer, one WhatsApp CTA with a named-contact slot. cards.name: OOH / billboard copy
cards.summary: Outdoor advertising copy for hoardings, bus shelters, metro and airport panels and digital (DOOH) screens: one idea in very few words, read in seconds from a distance or in motion, working together with one strong visual and a clearly visible brand. Good outdoor copy fits its site: shortest for highway hoardings, a little more where people wait (platforms, shelters), and often written for the place it stands.
use_for: city and highway hoardings
metro, bus-shelter, railway and airport transit panels
DOOH screens, including time-, weather- or location-triggered versions
local-business, real-estate and retail outdoor campaigns, including regional-language hoardings
avoid: Paragraphs, bullet lists or several messages. One idea per board; a series of boards can carry a sequence.

Phone numbers, long URLs and 'link in bio' on drive-by sites: nobody can note them at speed. Use the brand name people can search, a short memorable handle, or a QR code only where people stand and wait.
A tiny logo. If the brand is not readable at the same glance as the line, the board advertises the category, not the brand.
Puns that need a second read on highways. Save layered wordplay for dwell placements (metro platforms, airport gates).
English-only copy outside the metros by default. Regional-language hoardings are common outside the big cities; write in the language the area reads.

cards.goal: The passer-by notices the board, gets the single idea and remembers the brand; where the site allows, they act (take the next exit, scan, walk in).

structure.does: Where the board is, viewing distance and dwell time (highway at speed vs metro platform), audience, and language of the area.
The one idea: a benefit, a contrast, a local truth or a provocation, in the fewest words that carry it.
structure.length: drive-by: about 3-8 words; dwell sites: up to about 15

structure.does: The single image that completes the line (the product, a situation, a face), described for the designer.
Logo or pack shot large enough to read at the same glance as the headline.
Location direction ('2 km ahead, left'), a short handle, or a QR code at dwell sites only.
3-5 lines for testing or a site series; contextual DOOH versions (morning vs night, rain vs heat) where the screen supports it.

length.note: The headline itself is a handful of words; the deliverable also carries the site brief, visual direction and variants, which drive the total. Highway boards sit at the short end of every range; dwell placements allow a second line.

checklist: Does each board carry exactly one idea?
Is each drive-by headline short enough to read in a single glance?
Is the brand named or shown on every board, readable at the same glance as the line?
Is the visual described and does the line depend on it (rather than repeating it)?
Are phone numbers, long URLs and 'link in bio' kept off drive-by boards?
Is the language right for the area the board stands in?
Do the variants differ in idea, not just wording?
Are comparative or 'No. 1' claims substantiated or removed?
pitfalls: Writing on a laptop screen and judging it there. Shrink the layout to thumbnail size or view it from across the room; if the line or brand is unreadable, cut words.
Ignoring local sensitivities in topical or provocative boards (religion, regional pride, politics). One photographed hoarding can become a national controversy.
Copy that fights the site: a 'Slow down and enjoy' line on a congested flyover reads as mockery. Visit or Street View the site before finalising.

Not your shoes.' is a WEH line built on the site's real truth; three drive-by lines under 8 words, two dwell lines with a QR line, brand on every board, visuals that now match the lines (shoes in puddles, not sandals), a claim check for the dry-feet promise, and a natural Hinglish dwell line ('Baarish ka mood kharab hai. cards.name: Opinion column / op-ed
cards.summary: A signed argument that takes one clear position on a current issue and defends it with evidence for a publication's readers: a news peg, a thesis stated early, two or three reasons with proof, the strongest counterargument answered fairly, and a specific recommendation. Good op-eds argue one thing well, in the author's own credible voice, rather than surveying an issue.
use_for: op-eds and guest columns for newspapers' edit pages and news sites
ghostwritten op-eds for founders, executives, doctors, academics and policy experts
regular columns in publications and newsletters
opinion pieces adapted for LinkedIn articles or Substack
avoid: Fence-sitting ('there are pros and cons'). State the position in the first few paragraphs and argue it.
Covering five arguments thinly. Pick the two or three strongest and give each real evidence.
A product pitch dressed as an opinion. Editors reject it and readers distrust it; argue for a policy or practice, and disclose the author's interest in the bio line.
Attacking people instead of positions. Criticise decisions and records with evidence; personal imputations invite defamation claims.
No news peg. Tie the argument to something happening now (a ruling, a budget, a report, an anniversary) so the editor has a reason to run it this week.

cards.goal: The reader accepts, or seriously reconsiders, the author's position and the action it calls for; first, the editor accepts the piece.

structure.does: The argument as a claim ('India's cities should publish bus data. Here's why'). Editors often rewrite it; still supply one.
The news peg, or a vivid scene or fact that makes the issue urgent now.
The position in one or two plain sentences.
Why this author can speak on it (work, research, lived experience), woven into the text in a clause.
Two or three reasons, each with evidence: data with its source, an example, a precedent from another state or country.
The strongest opposing point stated fairly, then answered with evidence or a concession plus a reason the thesis still holds.
A specific action by a specific actor (a ministry, a regulator, companies, readers).
Return to the lede's scene or restate the stakes in a fresh line.
Author name, role, and any interest that needs disclosing.

length.note: The publication's own submission guidelines set the limit and any exclusivity terms; check them before writing and cut to fit rather than asking the editor to.

checklist: Is there a news peg in the first two paragraphs?
Is the thesis stated plainly by paragraph three?
Does every argument carry evidence with a named source?
Is the strongest counterargument stated fairly and answered?
Is there a specific recommendation naming who should act?
Is the piece one argument rather than a survey of the issue?
Is the author's standing established in the text or bio?
Is any conflict of interest disclosed in the bio line?
Is it within the target publication's word limit?
Does it criticise positions and decisions rather than people's character?
pitfalls: Ghostwriting without the author's actual view. Interview the author for their position, examples and the line they would never say; an op-ed the author cannot defend on a panel will embarrass them.
Sending the same piece to several outlets at once when they expect exclusivity. Pitch one at a time, with a short pitch note, and move on after their stated response window.
White-paper tone (passive voice, jargon, hedged claims). Read it aloud; every sentence should sound like the author arguing at a dinner table.
Stale statistics. Use the latest official figure and say its year; an old number undermines the whole argument.
